text: It was once believed that development was either continuous or discontinuous, but not both. <break time="0.8s" /> Today, scientists agree that development includes both continuity and discontinuity. <break time="0.8s" /> Whether a particular developmental change appears continuous or discontinuous depends in part on our point of view. <break time="0.8s" /> Consider physical growth. <break time="0.8s" /> We often think of increases in height as involving a slow and steady process, each month, an infant is taller than the prior month, illustrating continuous change. <break time="0.8s" /> However, when researchers measured infants height every day, they discovered that infants have growth days and nongrowth days, days in which they show rapid change in height mixed in with days in which there is no change in height, illustrating discontinuous change. <break time="0.8s" /> In this example, monthly measurements of infant height suggest gradual increases, but daily measurements show spurts of growth, each lasting 24 hours or less. <break time="0.8s" /> Thus, whether a given phenomenon, such as height, is described as continuous or discontinuous can vary depending on the perspective. <break time="0.8s" /> Most developmental scientists agree that some aspects of development are best described as continuous and others as discontinuous.
